rationale: A wins because it treats holes as holes instead of laundering them into claims. Its line, "which specific tools Linear expects teams to replace or run alongside, since the update doesn't name any competitor," is exactly the discipline this update needs. B is cleaner on the page, but "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" turns "no enterprise sales team is mentioned" into an enterprise-motion claim, and that is how a reporter kills you in one follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "engineering-only interface" overstates the fact pattern; Linear is known for engineering teams, but the update does not prove the interface was engineering-only.
"historically sold top-down to VPs" imports market lore that is not in the update. It may be true, but it needs sourcing before it can carry the contrarian angle.
"Another roadmapping tool arrives for product teams already drowning in software" is a useful service-journalism shape, but "drowning in software" is an unsupported trend claim.
"with no enterprise sales team in sight" leans past the supplied fact. The safer wording is that no enterprise sales team is mentioned and must be confirmed.
gaps_in_B: "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" is the worst overclaim in either set. The update says nothing about enterprise selling.
"Jira, Asana, Notion, and Monday" are plausible category names, but they are not in the update. B should have asked for competitors instead of decorating the pitch with them.
"the slower, more visual, more collaborative way non-engineers work" is a stereotype presented as context. It needs user evidence or a tighter phrasing.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is the wrong first move if no journalist list exists yet. Pick the angle, prove it, then build or vet names.
